coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: margin bridge, three root causes, sized levers, sequencing, decisions. Y's storyline is tighter, but its governing thought says fixing promotions, shrink and delivery 'gets Harlow to ~3%', while its own numbers need stores, labor, private label and stretch levers to reach 2.8–3.1%. X's governing thought names all the levers and the 2.9–3.1% range precisely, and each slide title matches its numbers. X's weakness is slide 3, which presents the team's own 'commercial fixes alone' hypothesis as the initial answer, and an executive summary that puts the labor-cut rebuttal under 'first moves'. These flaws roughly offset.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend a defensible R1/R2-type plan and reject the draft plan. X weighs more alternatives with numbers: the draft plan at 0.9–1.7%, the plan without the three board-vote stores at 2.7%, and exiting home delivery at ~3.3% but breaching the owners' commitment. X also gives low/base/high cases (2.0%/2.9%/3.8%), stage gates, a sized contingency, and a one-time budget of $20.1M against the $25M cap. X nets a 1% volume loss out of the promotion lever and keeps its labor trim small (3% of hours, with 1% reinvested in the leanest stores). Y has good touches: renegotiate rent before closing, cut promotions outside ValuMart areas first, and absorb the full wage rise. But Y leaves every one-time cost except the $7.5M uncosted while claiming $17.5M headroom. Y's targeted cut is larger (8% of hours in half the stores, +$6.8M) and its own shrink risk is not sized. Y also assumes no volume loss from the promotion cut. X's assumption that half the wage step is recovered in prices is optimistic given price perception, but it is flagged and stressed in the low case.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: the bridge (−$15.3M gross margin, −$12.6M e-commerce, −$4.5M labor, −$3.0M occupancy), e-commerce at −$10.4M, the fee test at about $2.5M, store exits at $6.6M, and the target gap. Both rebut the 6.1% claim and the category team's comp claim with a break-even calculation. Y adds a robustness check that e-commerce breaks even only above ~70% incrementality, and it makes fewer invented assumptions. Y's weak points are valuing promotions at the full $7.9M with no volume loss while calling its assumptions cautious, and stating headroom on uncosted items. X uses more of the pack: the vendor-funding decline, a wage/hours decomposition, per-order break-evens, sensitivities, and a net-of-volume promotion value. X's vendor-funding sizing (markdowns ≈ 25.9% of promoted sales) and its $10M shrink giveback rest on shaky inferences, though both are flagged, and the vendor lever is set to zero in the low case. X's covenant argument uses a run-rate rather than a fiscal-year figure; Y's in-year FY2026 build is more direct. Both flag the timing ambiguity.

revision.reasons: Both revise management's wage hypothesis from the quantified bridge (labor is 13% of the decline, because fewer hours offset the 9.4% wage rise). Both replace the blanket 8% cut with a targeted trim, and both reject a freeze-only approach to e-commerce in favour of repricing. X is more rigorous on the hypothesis itself. It lays out an explicit 'what would have to be true' test table and sizes the draft plan's net value as a range (+1.5 to +14.5, central ~4.5). It keeps only a small labor element, justified by the Q3–Q4 shrink similarity, with reinvestment in the leanest stores. X also tests and revises its own 'commercial fixes alone' hypothesis (2.1%). Y revises correctly too, showing the draft plan at ~1.5% and a shrink giveback of about half. But Y keeps a larger slice of the hours cut without sizing its shrink exposure. X's framing of the 'initial answer' as its own hypothesis rather than management's is slightly confusing.

overall.reasons: Both documents reach the right diagnosis and a defensible, sized plan that roughly reaches 3.0% with the covenant in view. X would serve the CEO and board better. It gives a costed one-time budget against the $25M cap, quantified alternatives including the delivery-exit and no-board-vote options, a scenario range, stage gates and a sized contingency. Its lever sizing is also more conservative on promotions (net of volume loss) and labor. Y is more concise, with some sharp points: the 70% break-even, rent renegotiation before closure, full wage absorption, and a direct FY2026 covenant build. But it leaves capital uncosted, sizes promotions with no volume loss, and proposes a larger labor cut without quantifying its shrink risk.
